blocks.p: Mercy Hall, Serenity. Return for the summer quarter, made on the ascension form.

Received into Mercy from the holding houses: fourteen. Released: fourteen. Received: none. Families told: fourteen. Resting lights lit: fourteen. Visits asked for: none. To reclamation: fourteen. Returned to the colony: water, five hundred and forty-one liters; carbon, one hundred and seventy-nine kilograms; trace metals, to stores. He has wiped away every tear from their eyes.
The church did its kindest work at the bottom of the ice, and no bishop Sol knew had ever gone down to see it.

He did not go back to bed. He sat in the refectory with a cup of tea going cold in front of him and the orange removed to the far end of the table, and when Pell came down at the first hour, fresh and pressed and pleasant, Sol was still sitting there. The tea was cold, and the clock over the door had moved further than he could account for. He had stopped, lately, quite trusting clocks.
“Your Grace. You’re up early.” Pell glanced at the cup, the untouched bread. “Did you sleep at all?”
“Pell. In sixty years, have you ever seen a release?”

The deacon considered it with real care, the way he considered everything Sol asked him. “Oh, no, Your Grace. Who has? But they say it’s the loveliest thing in the church.” He smiled. “That’s the beauty of it, isn’t it? Nobody is ever left behind sick. They all go up, and he makes them well.”
“Yes,” Sol said. “I suppose that’s the beauty of it.”
“Shall I bring your robe? The administrator’s office has sent over the Abundance records, and I thought this morning we might...”
“Start without me. I have something to see to at the holding house.”
“Of course, Your Grace.” Pell did not ask what. He never asked what.

When the deacon had gone, Sol touched his temple and called up his own custody record, which he had never in his life had cause to look at. The Halo laid it across the corner of his sight. It went on for a long time. Name after name, colony after colony, decade after decade, each form opened with the same line in the same type: Received into Mercy by the hand of Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. Beside each name was a status field. He let the list run, faster and faster, until the names blurred into a grey column like falling ash, and then he stopped it at random and read.
Released.

He let it run again and stopped it again. Released. A miner on Plenty, a hundred and ten years ago. A schoolteacher in Concord, nine years ago. A child, he saw, and did not let himself read the age. Released. Released. Released. It was the word in Sallow’s ledger, and the only word there was. He did not look for the other one. He had been told about the Face’s own door, and been satisfied.
He closed the list and finished the cold tea and went out.

The transport bay was at the bottom of the holding house, a long white room with a sealed door at one end where the tunnel began. The crawler was already there: a low white car on broad treads, its windows frosted, its flanks marked with the open hand of the Mercy Office. Three pods sat in a rack inside it, and two wardens in white were checking the seals. They straightened when they saw him.
“Your Grace.”
“I’d like to see the manifest.”

The senior warden passed it to his Halo without hesitation. Three names. A man from the ice mines on Serenity, reported by his supervisor. PRYOR, Della, from Abundance, reported by her neighbor: the young woman with the bruised forehead who had laid her palm on the glass yesterday and asked him when she could go home. He had told her Soon. It had been true. And a hydroponics technician from Concord, ASHBY, Nell, reported by a coworker, and received into Mercy five weeks ago by the hand of Sol Tarren.

The coworker’s statement ran to a line, as they always did. Gives her ration chits to the night crew. Talks with her eyes shut in the bean rows. Fell at the noon change. The first of those caught in him, and he could not think why, until he remembered a word he had written in his notes the night before and struck through. It still made no sense. He put it away.
He walked to the third pod and looked through the frosted glass.

She was young, or looked it, as everyone did. Dark hair cropped short, a scatter of freckles across her nose that Renewal had either left alone or put back on purpose. Her eyes were closed. Her lips were slightly parted. She looked like someone asleep on a long crossing, which was what she was.
He did not know her at all.

He had signed for her. The form said so. It would have come to him the way most of them came, a warden’s report from Concord laid in the corner of his sight while he was somewhere else, one of a dozen that week, and he had signed it with a thought between a homily and a dinner. He had never stood in the greenhouse among the bean vines with her head on somebody’s folded coat. He had never said note the time, or nothing in her mouth, or see that she’s comfortable. He searched his memory for her face anyway, for the room, for anything, and there was nothing there to find, because he had never once looked.
“She’s well sedated, Your Grace,” the warden said kindly. “She won’t wake till Mercy.”
“I’ll follow you down.”
The warden hesitated for the first time. “Of course, Your Grace. It’s not a long ride. It’s lovely, actually, if you’ve never been. Most of the episcopate never has.”

The church kept a car at the holding house for visiting clergy. Sol took it himself, without a driver, and when the bay door opened onto the tunnel he let the crawler go ahead and followed its red running lights down into the ice.
The wardens were right. It was lovely.

The tunnel bored down through the shell at a long gentle slope, lit at intervals by white lamps set into the walls, and between the lamps the ice glowed with a light of its own: blue near the surface, then deeper blue, then a blue so dark it was almost violet, the color of a held breath. Old cracks ran through it like veins in marble, and in places there were things trapped in it, bubbles and dust and pale threads of mineral, hanging motionless where they had hung for a hundred thousand years. The car hummed. The crawler’s lights went on ahead, steady and unhurried. Sol drove for forty minutes, down and down, and the cold came through the glass beside his face like a hand laid against it, and in all that time he did not see another vehicle or another soul.

Somewhere past the halfway lamps the old warning came behind his eye, and then the car was standing still. It had stopped itself, as such cars did when no hand was on the controls. His left hand lay flat against the window, numb with cold. The dash clock had moved on nine minutes, and in the cab, quite steady, he heard his own voice finishing something he had not known he was saying: “...a human hand on every burn.”
It was the old man’s phrase, he told himself. He drove on, faster than was wise, until the crawler’s red lights showed again far down in the blue.

He had always pictured the other half of Mercy Hall, the half that was not cradles, when he pictured it at all, as a small place: a chapel at the end of a corridor, a bed, a Pearl, a door the sick went through on their way up.
The tunnel opened into a cavern, and there it was.

It had been built into the ice the way a cathedral is built into a city, as though it had always been there and the ice had grown up around it. Its walls were white panels rising in long arches, lit softly from within, and its roof was the cavern’s ceiling, a vault of black-blue ice so far overhead that the lamps on it looked like stars. In the forecourt a fountain played. In Serenity’s gravity the water rose impossibly high, a slow white column, and fell back so gently that it seemed to be thinking about each drop. Over the great doors, cut into the ice in letters as tall as a man, was the line he had preached on a thousand times.
He has wiped away every tear from their eyes.
The crawler went around the side of the building to a low bay. Sol left the car in the forecourt and went in through the front.

The director of Mercy Hall met him in the atrium. She was a tall woman in the white of the Mercy Office, with a silver band at her collar and a face that looked perhaps forty and had probably looked forty for three hundred years. She came toward him with both hands out, and her hands, when she took his, were warm.

“Your Grace. Warden Kell. They called down from the transport; I couldn’t believe it. We so rarely have a bishop here.” She looked genuinely glad. “Will you take tea? You’ve come all that way through the cold.”
“I’d like to see the work,” Sol said. “If I may.”

“Of course you may. You of all people. Do you know how many of our patients have come to us under your hand?” She smiled, and there was nothing in the smile but warmth. “We’ve always been grateful for how gently you send them.”

He felt it reach him, the small warm pleasure of being known by name, which had met him at a thousand doors and which he had always let in, as one lets in a cat. He let it in now, and was glad, and would remember afterward that he had been glad.

She walked him through the Hall herself. It was very quiet. The floors were pale and soft underfoot, and there was music, as there was in the Bounty Market, from nowhere in particular. The corridors were wide and clean and smelled faintly of something green. They passed rooms with their doors open: an office, a records room, a small chapel with a Pearl in its wall, glowing. Every room was clean and still and waiting, the way a church is waiting on the morning of a feast.

At a branching of the corridor the light to the left was warmer, and the walls were painted with birds. Sol knew what lay down there; every bishop did. He had blessed a thousand of its cradles at a thousand haloing feasts. Mercy Hall had been the nursery of Serenity before it was anything else, and it was still: the colony’s children came up from that wing at nine weeks’ growing under the Halo and went home perfect, and none of them ever cried. Through a long window at the end he could see the rows of small clear cradles lit from within, very still. “Life comes in at that end,” Kell said, with real pride, “and goes up from this one.” She turned him to the right.

“Every patient is assessed first,” Kell said, in the tone of someone who has given this explanation to visiting committees and enjoys it. “We read their pattern against their last clean backup in Sion. The Virus shows as noise, Your Grace: a region of the mind the system simply cannot read. Like a fog on a lens. And everything the mind sees, it sees through the fog.”
“And it can’t be cleaned.”

“Not here. Not in the flesh.” She said it with gentle regret, as of a garden that would not grow in that soil. “The noise isn’t in one place. It runs all through the pattern, and the body holds it there the way a wound holds a splinter. No hand of ours can reach it. But his can.” She glanced up, as people did when they spoke of him, though there was only the vault of ice. “So we let them go up to him. Their own Halo carries them, and the Face takes them in by its own door, and lifts the noise out of them in the City, and they rest there until they’re whole. That’s all Mercy is, Your Grace. We open the door.”

They had stopped before a long window. Beyond it was a small room, white and warm, with a bed in it and a vase of flowers grown under lamps, and a chair for a warden to sit in. Above the bed a little Pearl was set into the wall, no larger than a hand, glowing gold.
“This is where they die,” Sol said.
“Release.” Kell’s voice was soft. “We don’t say the old words here. They’re the old world’s words, and there’s nothing of the old world in it. Watch. You’ll see.”
The door at the back of the room opened, and they brought Nell Ashby in.

She was awake, or nearly. Two wardens walked her between them, slowly, in the long floating steps of the moon’s gravity, and she leaned on them the way a child leans on its parents at the end of a long day. They sat her on the bed. One of them brought her a cup of something warm and held it while she drank. The other stroked her short hair back from her forehead and began, very quietly, to sing. Sol could hear it faintly through the glass. It was the cradle song every child in the worlds fell asleep to, the one he had sung over the infants he haloed: In the beginning was Life, and Life was the light of all people.
Nell looked up at the warden who was singing. Her lips moved.
Kell touched a panel by the window, and the faint singing stopped. “We don’t listen, Your Grace,” she said, almost apologetically. “For your protection. Even through glass.”

Sol watched the girl’s lips. He could not make out what she was saying. He knew only that it was not the cradle song. It had a different shape. She said it twice, looking up at the warden with something in her face he did not have a name for, and the warden went on stroking her hair and singing words she could no longer hear.

They helped her lie back. The singing warden kept her hand. The other touched two fingers to Nell’s temple, the way anyone touches the temple to call or to sign, and held them there, and Sol felt it at his own temple: a light pressure, two fingers’ worth, just where the coin lay under his skin. He did not lift his hand.

“The Halo does it,” Kell said. “Isn’t that a mercy, in itself? It’s been with her since the day she was born. It kept her alive through every crossing she ever made. It knows the way up better than any of us could. It quiets the mind first, and then the breath, and then the heart, and then it carries her. There’s no pain at all. There’s nothing to fear.”

Nell’s eyes closed. Her breathing slowed and deepened until she seemed to be sleeping, and then it slowed again. Sol watched her chest rise. He watched it fall. He waited for it to rise again, and it rose, much later, and fell, and he waited, and the warden holding her hand looked up at a screen on the wall, and nodded, and set the hand down on the blanket and smoothed the cloth beside it, the way one finishes making a bed.

Above the bed the little Pearl changed. Its gold softened and paled, slowly, as a lamp is turned down in a room where a child has fallen asleep, until it gave only a soft, even light, steady and very quiet. Sol had passed that light in a hundred alcoves. He had blessed one that week on the garden ring. He had never seen one lit.
“There,” Kell said, and her eyes were shining. “She’s gone up.”

They drew the sheet up over her face. In Serenity’s gravity it took a long time to settle, drifting down by slow degrees, the cloth finding the shape of her forehead and her nose and her chin as if it were learning them.
Then they wheeled the bed to a door at the back of the room, and the door opened, and closed, and the room was empty except for the chair and the flowers and the small soft light.
“Where does that door go?”

“Reclamation.” Kell said it plainly; there was no shame in her anywhere. “Water, carbon, the trace metals. Serenity wastes nothing. Below us is the sea, Your Grace, the whole dark sea of this world, and every drop that comes up from it is precious. Everything returns.” She smiled. “She has no more need of it. She’s with him.”
“And her family?”
“Are told that she’s in Mercy. Resting. Tonight they’ll see that light in their own Pearl.” She nodded at the wall. “When he’s finished with her, she’ll come to them.”
Somewhere on Concord, then, a mother would kneel tonight and find a soft light at the end of her alcove where a daughter had been, and lay a place at the table, and be content.
Kell touched his sleeve. “You’ve gone pale. It moves everyone, the first time. It moved me, a very long time ago. But you see there are no tears in it. Nothing was done in anger. Nobody was hurt.”
Sol looked at the empty room through the glass. The chair. The flowers. The light.
He tried to call it mercy, and found that it was not hard.

He was a learned man, and he did it carefully, the way he would have built a homily. The Virus was a sickness of the mind, and it spread; he had seen the mothers cover their children’s ears. It could not be healed in the flesh, so the church did not leave the sick in the flesh to suffer it. It gave them a warm cup, and a hand held, and a song, and sent them up to the only physician who could reach the place where the sickness was. There was no fear in the room, no pain, no cruelty. Death shall be no more. And this was not death, not as the old world had meant it, with its terror and its graves and its weeping in the car. This was a door, and a light beyond it. Every piece of it was what the church had always said it was. Nothing had been hidden from him. He had only never come to look, and he had come now, and it was beautiful. The old man under the ice was wrong.
It nearly held. He stood at the glass and felt it nearly hold.

But he had signed for her, and he had never seen her face until today. And she had looked up at the singing warden and said something twice that was not the cradle song, and no one in the building had heard it. And there was still, very faintly, two fingers’ weight at his temple, where nothing touched him at all.
“How many?” he said.
“Since the Hall was opened?” Kell tilted her head. “I’d have to look. We don’t keep the number on the wall, Your Grace. It isn’t a number anyone needs.”

He could have told her, to the one, how many souls he had sent up from the bier. He had never counted the ones he had sent up from here. He thought of his custody list running grey in the corner of his sight, faster and faster, like ash. Released. A miner. A schoolteacher. A child. He did the arithmetic without wanting to, the way his mind did arithmetic, and then he stopped it, the way he had stopped the list.
“Thank you, Warden,” he said. “You’ve been very kind.”

“It’s what we’re for.” She walked with him back toward the atrium, unhurried, her hands folded. At the great doors she paused. “Since you’re here, Your Grace, may I trouble you with one of your own? It would save us sending it up.”
“One of mine.”

“The Hale case. The old man from Abundance.” She said it without any particular weight, a clerk mentioning a file. “He’s scheduled for tomorrow, the second hour. You signed his custody, so the release needs your countersign. Usually we send it to you and you sign from wherever you are. But some bishops like to attend their own. It gives the families comfort, when there are families.”
Something opened in the corner of his sight. He had not touched his temple; she had sent it. A form, plain and white, in the same type as all the others.
Release. HALE, Stephen. Custody: Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life.
Beneath it, a blank line, waiting.
“Can it be delayed?” he said. His voice sounded quite ordinary.

Kell’s brows rose a little. “The schedule comes to us from Concord, Your Grace, and Concord’s comes from Sion. Ordinarily a bishop might petition. But this one came down already flagged.” She looked at him with mild, untroubled curiosity. “He’s refused Renewal, you know. Over and over. The wardens up top say he talks to them through the glass all day long, though of course no one listens. He’s very old.” She smiled. “Think of it. By tomorrow evening he’ll be young again. It will be a kindness. You’ll see.”

He thought of the old man on the edge of his bed with his back to the Pearl, saying Sol as if it were a word he had kept safe for a long time. In the City he would be young, and whatever the noise was in him would be lifted out by a hand that did not tremble: the rain that ruined his shoes, the noodles at three in the morning, the bishop he said he had once known. He would rest in a soft light at the end of someone’s table, if anyone laid him a place, and no one would call on him, because no one did.
Sol did not want it. He could not have said, in any word the church had given him, why not.

The fountain played in the forecourt, slow and white, each drop rising and falling as if it had all the time in the world. Sol walked past it to the car and got in and sat with his hands on the controls.

He did not sign the form. He did not close it either. All the long way up through the ice, through the violet and the deep blue and the blue, it hung in the corner of his sight, patient and white, the way it had waited for him a thousand times before, for nothing more than a thought.
